oneliner.t: Allagash logger and former Maine Senate president (2018–2024) who was picked as the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee at a July 25, 2026 party convention after primary winner Graham Platner withdrew; he faces Sen. Susan Collins.

upbringing.t: Jackson was born in Fort Kent and raised in Allagash, a town of a few hundred people on the Canadian border. His mother, Colleen McBreairty, a teacher, had him at 16; his father, Joe Jackson, was a logger, and the two divorced when he was in middle school. At 12 he saw his father and other northern Maine loggers strike over mechanized harvesting and wages. He began logging at 19, working long shifts, often without health insurance. In 1998 he helped lead a week-long blockade of Maine–Canada border crossings to protest the hiring of Canadian loggers over Maine workers, which ended without success and led him into politics.

education.school: University of Maine at Fort Kent

career.role: Maine state representative (elected as an independent in 2002, Democrat from 2004); chaired the Fisheries and Wildlife Committee
Maine state senator; assistant majority leader (2012), majority leader (July 2013–Dec. 2014)
Maine state senator; minority leader (2016–2018), Senate president (Dec. 2018–Dec. 2024); left because of term limits

platform.t: Medicare for All; a moratorium on private-equity purchases of independent medical practices.
Abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE); opposes the 2026 ICE funding.
Overturn Citizens United; says he rejects corporate PAC money in this race.
Calls Israel's war in Gaza a genocide; calls for ending U.S. military aid to Israel and opposes a 'blank check'; calls Netanyahu a war criminal.
Opposes the 2026 Iran war; says the U.S. must leave to bring down fuel and heating costs.
Supports abortion rights and codifying them in federal law ('abortion is healthcare').
Union rights; higher taxes on top earners; campaigns against billionaires and corporations.

(From his 2026 governor's race) bar out-of-state private-equity and multi-state real-estate firms from buying starter homes; a higher lodging tax on out-of-state visitors and a luxury tax on vacation homes over $1 million.

promises.t: Never vote for U.S. taxpayer-funded military aid to Israel.

claims.claim: His mother was 16 when he was born.

record.t: Wikipedia says the same, but no primary record was checked; it appears to rest on his own account.

claims.claim: His father, grandfather and great-grandfather were loggers.

record.t: AP and Wikipedia describe him as a fifth-generation logger; Wikipedia names his father, Joe Jackson, as a logger. The earlier generations rest on his own account.

claims.claim: Became a logger, running equipment, driving trucks and cutting wood.

record.t: AP: began work as a lumberjack at 19, with 12-hour shifts often starting at 2:30 a.m.; a co-worker is quoted.

claims.claim: Took part in a border blockade protesting billionaire landowners cutting loggers' wages; politicians including first-term Sen. Collins promised to listen but did not follow through.

record.t: The 1998 blockade is documented. AP and Wikipedia describe its target as the hiring of lower-paid Canadian loggers over Maine workers, not landowner wage cuts as such, and police escorted him away. Collins's alleged unkept promise was not found in the record.

claims.claim: Served about twenty years in the Maine Legislature, including six years as Senate President.

record.t: House Dec. 2002–Dec. 2008; Senate Dec. 2008–Dec. 2014 and Dec. 2016–Dec. 2024 (20 years); Senate president Dec. 5, 2018–Dec. 4, 2024.

He sponsored a 2017 generic-access law (enacted 2018 without Gov. LePage's signature) and 2019 laws creating a prescription drug affordability board and allowing importation, signed by Gov. Mills. No price-effect data was checked.

claims.claim: Passed some of the strongest reproductive health protections in the country.

record.t: Documented: 2019 abortion-coverage law and a 2023 law allowing abortion at any stage if a doctor deems it medically necessary. 'Strongest' is a characterization. Earlier in his career he had perfect Maine Right to Life scores (2003, 2010).

claims.claim: Passed universal school meals; delivered property tax relief; expanded rural health care.

record.t: No legislative record for these items was opened in this pass.

claims.claim: Earned an associate's degree from the University of Maine at Fort Kent in 2000.

record.t: Wikipedia lists an A.A. in business from UMFK (year not given).

claims.claim: Lives in Allagash with his partner, Lana, and has two adult sons.

record.t: AP and Wikipedia agree. A 2023 complaint that he lived outside his district (based on a 2019 Augusta home purchase) was dismissed unanimously by the Maine Ethics Commission, which found insufficient evidence he lived anywhere but Allagash.

claims.claim: Collins votes with Trump 96% of the time.

record.t: BDN: the figure is misleading and out of date — a CQ-Roll Call analysis of only those bills where Trump took an explicit position (95% for the first seven months of 2025), when leaders mostly brought up bills he backed.

claims.claim: Collins voted five times against ending the Iran war.

record.t: Of 14 war-powers votes since February 2026, she voted against five; she later voted to end the war after the April 30 deadline, so the count is accurate but incomplete.

claims.claim: Mainer calls out Susan Collins for advancing $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts.

said.where: campaign TV ad (listed on campaign news page)

record.t: Collins voted to advance the 2025 tax-and-spending bill (June 29, 2025) but voted against final passage. The $1 trillion figure was not checked against CBO here.

claims.claim: Collins has spent 25 years avoiding public town halls.

record.t: No count of Collins's public town halls was found; her campaign says she prefers individual and small-group meetings.

claims.claim: Collins and her husband are profiting from the Iran war.

record.t: The Maine Independent reported her husband owns Boeing and RTX stock; her spokesperson says Collins has owned no individual stock as a senator and an adviser manages his investments. No record shows profit from the war, and a spouse's holdings are not hers.

said.t: Says he rejects corporate PAC money in the Senate race.

did.t: FEC records for his 2026 Senate committee show PAC money only from labor, leadership, membership and ideological PACs (no corporate PACs). The Washington Post reported that a PAC he used accepted corporate and pharmaceutical money until about two years ago, and his 2014 House campaign took $2,250 from corporate PACs and $500 from a trade PAC.

said.t: Said he would not accept AIPAC funding.

did.t: No AIPAC or other pro-Israel PAC contributions appear in his FEC committee records (2014 or 2026).

entries.t: Perfect score from Maine Right to Life (also 2010).
Helped pass a law allowing abortion at any stage if a doctor deems it medically necessary; now says 'abortion is healthcare' and that he made mistakes early on.
One of two Senate Democrats to vote against legalizing same-sex marriage.
100% rating from Equality Maine; says he regrets the 2009 vote.
Said little publicly about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict during his legislative career.
Called the Gaza war a genocide and called for ending U.S. military aid to Israel.
Opposed a 'blank check' for Israel; said he did not want more offensive weapons sent; called Netanyahu a war criminal.
Ran for the Maine House as a Republican and lost (2,172–2,017).
His House campaign received $1,500 from the NRA Political Victory Fund.
After the 2023 Lewiston shootings, led gun bills including a 72-hour waiting period and a bump-stock ban; in 2025 backed the red-flag referendum.

aipac_endorse.t: Not endorsed; he says he won't accept AIPAC funding (as of 2026-10-14). J Street endorsed him.

aipac_pac.note: career — no AIPAC PAC contributions in his FEC committee records (2014 House run and 2026 Senate run); Track AIPAC itself was not reachable

statements.t: Used the word 'genocide' for Israel's war in Gaza and called on his campaign site for ending U.S. military aid to Israel.
Vowed he would never vote for U.S. taxpayer-funded military aid to Israel.

In a News Center Maine interview, said some Maine Jews avoid the word genocide because of the Holocaust; he then apologized for a generalization about Jewish Mainers, without changing his view of the war.
In the first debate, opposed a 'blank check' for Israel, called Netanyahu a war criminal, and cited his J Street endorsement.

note.t: His only federal financial disclosures are House candidate reports from his 2014 run (scanned; read by OCR). They list State of Maine legislative salary (about $15.6K in the preceding year), small bank accounts, a joint U.S. Department of Education loan for a child's student loans, and a Maine PERS legislative pension (eligible at 62, about $3,400 a year). No securities, no outside positions. A 2026 Senate candidate financial disclosure was not checked (Senate eFD not reachable).

debates.note: Agreed to four televised debates in October 2026 (Oct. 6, 8, 13, 15); did not respond to the CNN/BDN invitation; pushed for town-hall formats.

townhalls.period: Sept. 2026 (Lewiston, Gorham, Jay, plus one his campaign calls his 'fourth')

note.t: Born in Fort Kent (1968) and has lived in Allagash; he also bought a house in Augusta in 2019 for legislative sessions. No documented period of living outside Maine.

checks.legal: No direct CourtListener/Justia search (not reachable from this tool). News search for ethics complaints and lawsuits: found only the 2023 Maine Ethics Commission complaint (dismissed). No criminal or civil cases found in the sources read.
checks.foreign: FARA bulk-file exact-name search (provided public records): no matches. 2013/2014 House candidate disclosures: no foreign assets, income or positions. No foreign-government or foreign-business ties in news read.
checks.claims: Mechanical sample: (a) every checkable claim on jacksonformaine.com/about (10 rated, some grouped); (b) the issues page (jacksonformaine.com/priorities) could not be opened by this tool, so platform claims were not rated; substituted his fact-checked claims from the Oct. 6 debate (BDN/PolitiFact) and one from the Oct. 8 debate; (c) ad spend unknown and ads not covered by news, so the campaign's own ad list was used (Medicaid ad rated); plus his town-hall claim about Collins.
checks.democracy: Not in Congress for any certification vote. Did not search specifically for statements on the 2020/2024 presidential results.

legal.t: Rep. John Andrews (R) filed a complaint alleging he lived outside his Senate district, citing a 2019 federal mortgage that listed an Augusta house as his primary residence. On Oct. 25, 2023 the five-member Maine Ethics Commission voted unanimously not to investigate, finding insufficient evidence that he lived anywhere but Allagash. Andrews said he would ask the U.S. attorney to look into the mortgage forms; no federal action was found.

recordx.note: Not a sitting member, so no missed-vote figure. His 2014 House candidate report was posted by the Clerk on 5/23/2014 (scanned stamp partly illegible), so on-time filing could not be confirmed. FEC notices/RFAIs for his committees were not checked. His 2014 House committee ended the cycle with cash on hand of -$253.47 per FEC totals. Fewer than two recordx items could be documented.

corp.t: His 2014 House campaign took $2,250 from corporate PACs (Avangrid, FairPoint Communications, EDP Renewables) and $500 from a trade PAC (American Sportfishing Association). The Washington Post reported that a PAC he used accepted corporate and pharmaceutical money until about two years ago. No corporate PAC money appears in his 2026 Senate committee records.

research_notes: NOMINATION: Graham Platner won the June 9, 2026 Democratic primary (72.1%) and withdrew July 8–10 after sexual-assault allegations, which he denies. Jackson, who had finished third in the June 9 governor's primary (21.1% first round, eliminated in round 3), was nominated by the party convention in Bangor on July 25, 566–5 over Saundra Pelletier. MONEY: The Senate committee had $0 through June 30, 2026 (it formed after that); the first full report (Q3) is due Oct. 15. ActBlue data reported by Maine Morning Star placed him third among Democratic Senate candidates for July 2026, with no dollar figure given. Committee contributions and coordinated party spending after June 30 come from donor committees' own reports. Coordinated party expenditures (DSCC $366,120; Maine Democratic Party $17,557) are not receipts. Independent-expenditure figures are raw line-item sums. 'Government That Works PAC' (hybrid PAC; $1.65M pro-Jackson) was not identified further. CLAIMS: Wikipedia cites a Maine Wire (conservative outlet) headline saying he accused Allagash officials of rigging the 2023 selectman vote that he lost by six votes (a recount confirmed the loss); this was not independently confirmed, so it is not entered under democracy. Also not entered: Collins's remark about his partner's family relationship (personal, not a record item). RELATIVES: none of the findings rely on a relative's record. FEC 2014 'indiv' and 'pac' figures are from FEC totals. Photo omitted (no Wikimedia file URL opened).
